newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan warns businessmen of risks in South Africa.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan warns businessmen of risks in South Africa.

text.p: Taiwan on Sunday warned its businessmen of potential investment risks in South Africa, the same day Taipei and Pretoria were scheduled to hold a new round of talks on future ties.

Cho Shih-chao, a deputy director of the economics ministry, told the state-run Central News Agency that Taiwanese investors could face investment risks after South Africa severs ties with the island by the end of 1997.
South African President Nelson Mandela announced last November that Pretoria, the biggest of Taiwan's diplomatic allies, would switch ties to mainland China this year.
Taiwanese firms should "carefully evaluate" their investment projects in South Africa before Taipei and Pretoria signed an investment protection pact, the agency quoted Cho as saying.
The government would "adjust" its economic policies toward South Africa and investment activities originally aimed at cementing ties would be reconsidered, the agency reported.
Taiwan has suspended all aid projects and treaties in protest against the decision to break diplomatic ties.
Cho was quoted as saying he would not be surprised to see many Taiwan-funded firms -- especially money-losing textile companies -- terminate their operations in South Africa soon.

Foreign Minister John Chang, who was scheduled hold a new round of talks with South African officials in Pretoria on Sunday, also hinted that Taiwan investors in South Africa should look for alternatives.

"South Africa has many problems of it own. We are still uncertain about whether its economic development and investment environment will improve or deteriorate in the future," Chang said in Swaziland on Saturday in a broadcast on state television.
"There are many other alternatives, this place (Swaziland) is one of them," Chang said.
"I have no intenion of asking Taiwan businessmen in South Africa to withdraw because this will affect our negotiations. But South Africa has to prove it has a good investment environment."
About 280 Taiwanese factories in South Africa have decided to close temporarily to pressure the government into restoring diplomatic ties with Taiwan, South Africa's state television said on Friday.

The factories, affiliated with the Association of Chinese Industrialists in Southern Africa, told a news programme they were uncertain about their future in South Africa and needed diplomatic offices to protect them.
Nearly 300 Taiwan businesses have operations in South Africa with total investment topping $1.5 billion. At least 43,000 jobs are created through Taiwanese investment.

Most of the 30 countries that recognise Taiwan's Republic of China government rather than the Communist People's Republic of China on the mainland are underdeveloped states in central America and Africa.

Communist China, Taiwan's arch-rival since a civil war split them in 1949, regards the island as a rebel province not entitled to foreign ties. It has tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in its quest to bring Taiwan under mainland rule.
